title: Community-acquired pneumonia: severity, antibiotics, and follow-up

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2019 ATS/IDSA community-acquired pneumonia guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which items make up the CURB-65 score?
a: Blood pressure under 90 systolic or 60 diastolic
questions.why: A score of 0 or 1 usually means outpatient care; 2, consider admission; 3 or more, admission and consideration of intensive care. The Pneumonia Severity Index is the guideline's preferred alternative.

questions.q: Which are appropriate for outpatient pneumonia in a healthy adult with no recent antibiotics?
questions.why: A macrolide alone is a third option only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is under 25%, which excludes most of the United States. Ciprofloxacin does not cover pneumococcus.

questions.q: Outpatient pneumonia in a patient with COPD and diabetes. Which regimen fits?
questions.a: Amoxicillin-clavulanate plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
questions.why: Comorbidity widens the likely organisms. A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers everything alone but carries tendon, nerve and aortic warnings, so the combination is usually preferred.

questions.q: What is the standard regimen for a patient admitted with non-severe pneumonia?
questions.a: A beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone plus a macrolide
questions.why: A respiratory fluoroquinolone alone is the alternative. Severe pneumonia gets the same beta-lactam and macrolide, with the macrolide preferred over a fluoroquinolone.

questions.q: When is empirical MRSA or Pseudomonas cover added in community-acquired pneumonia?
a: Prior isolation of the organism from the respiratory tract
Hospitalisation with intravenous antibiotics in the past 90 days, with locally validated risk
d: Any patient admitted to the ward
questions.why: The old healthcare-associated pneumonia category was retired because it drove broad antibiotics without benefit. Cultures and a nasal MRSA swab allow rapid de-escalation.

questions.q: What is the minimum duration of antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia?
questions.why: Stability means afebrile for 48 hours with normal vital signs. Longer courses are for MRSA, Pseudomonas, or complications such as empyema.

questions.q: Should blood and sputum cultures be sent for an outpatient with pneumonia?
questions.why: They are sent for severe pneumonia, and for anyone being treated for or at risk of MRSA or Pseudomonas. A urinary Legionella antigen is added in severe cases and outbreaks.

questions.q: Can a low procalcitonin be used to withhold antibiotics in a patient with a clinical and radiographic diagnosis of pneumonia?
d: Yes, if the chest radiograph is unclear
questions.why: Procalcitonin misses a proportion of bacterial pneumonias. It can help decide when to stop, not whether to start.

questions.q: A patient with pneumonia tests positive for influenza. What is added?
questions.a: Oseltamivir, regardless of how long symptoms have lasted, if admitted
d: Oseltamivir only within 48 hours of onset
questions.why: The 48-hour window applies to outpatients with uncomplicated influenza. Admitted patients benefit later than that, and the antibiotic continues because bacterial co-infection is common.

questions.q: Suspected aspiration pneumonia in a patient with dysphagia. Is anaerobic coverage added?
questions.a: Not routinely; only with a lung abscess or empyema
questions.why: Aspiration pneumonia is treated with the usual community regimen. Aspiration pneumonitis, the chemical injury from gastric contents, often needs no antibiotic at all.

questions.q: A patient has recovered from pneumonia within a week. Is a follow-up chest radiograph needed?
questions.why: The guideline dropped routine follow-up imaging. It is reasonable in smokers over 50 or where symptoms persist, since a mass can hide behind a resolving infection.

questions.q: Are corticosteroids recommended for non-severe community-acquired pneumonia?
d: Yes, if there is a fever
questions.why: They are reserved for refractory septic shock, and more recent trials support them only in severe pneumonia. In non-severe disease they add hyperglycaemia and readmissions.
